intro: English has one little verb for I am. Spanish has two. When you say who you are, where you are from or what you are like, you use ser: Soy Maya. Soy de Chicago. When you say how you feel or where you are right now, you use estar: Estoy cansada. Estoy en la escuela.

In this unit you will read a pen-pal letter from Monterrey and spend a long day at a county fair. You will learn the five forms of each verb, match -o and -a endings, and ask ¿De dónde eres? and ¿Cómo estás?
By the end you will be able to introduce yourself, describe a friend, say how you feel, tell where you are, and choose between ser and estar with a simple rule of thumb.
bigQuestion: Why does Spanish need two verbs for to be, and how do you know which one to use?

test.why: Where you are from uses ser, and yo takes soy.

test.q: Choose the right word: Hoy nosotros ___ cansados.

She is happy with my friend.

choices: Mi mamá es en la casa.
Mi mamá está en la casa.
test.why: Where someone is uses estar: está en la casa.

test.q: How do you ask a friend How are you?
test.why: ¿Cómo estás? uses estar and asks how someone feels.

test.q: A boy says he is tall. Which is right?
test.why: Tall is what you are like, so use ser, and a boy takes -o.

test.q: Which is spelled the Spanish way?
test.why: Nationality words are lowercase, and a group adds -s.

test.q: Choose the right word: Tú ___ muy inteligente.
test.why: Smart is a trait, so use ser, and tú takes eres.

test.q: What does Chicago está en Illinois mean?
test.why: Estar plus en tells where a place is.

test.q: Sara is sad today. Which is right?
test.why: A feeling today uses estar, and Sara takes está.

test.q: Which form of estar goes with ellos?
test.why: Ellos, ellas and ustedes take están.

test.q: My uncle is a cook. Which is right?
test.why: Jobs use ser with no un, and a man is cocinero.

test.q: Which question asks where someone is from?
test.why: ¿De dónde eres? uses ser and de to ask where you are from.

test.q: Leo y Ana ___ en la feria.

test.q: What is the rule of thumb for estar?
choices: Use it for your name and job.
Use it for where you are from.
Use it for how you feel and where you are.
Use it for what you look like.

write.prompt: Write 4 to 6 sentences in Spanish to introduce yourself to a pen pal. Say who you are and where you are from (ser), what you are like (ser), how you feel today (estar), and where you are right now (estar).
tips: Use soy for your name, where you are from and what you are like.
Use estoy for how you feel and where you are.
Match -o or -a on each describing word to you.
Check accents: estás, está, están, and ¿De dónde?
Read it aloud to a partner before you finish.

title: Soy and Estoy

chapters.title: Ser: Who and What I Am
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you tell someone who you are, where you are from, and what you are like in Spanish?

story.title: A Letter from Monterrey
story.kicker: A girl in Mexico writes to a new pen pal in Chicago, and every line uses one small verb.
paragraphs: Maya is in fourth grade in Chicago. Her class has pen pals in Monterrey, a big city in northern Mexico. One morning her teacher hands out envelopes. Maya's letter is from a girl named Lucía. The first line says ¡Hola, Maya! (Hi, Maya!).

Lucía writes: Me llamo Lucía. Soy de Monterrey. (My name is Lucía. I am from Monterrey.) Then she writes: Soy alta y soy simpática. (I am tall and I am nice.) Maya reads soy three times. She guesses it means I am.

Next Lucía writes about her family. Mi papá es maestro. (My dad is a teacher.) Mi hermano es muy cómico. (My brother is very funny.) Nosotros somos mexicanos. (We are Mexican.) Now Maya sees es and somos too.

At the end Lucía asks a question: ¿Y tú? ¿Cómo eres? (And you? What are you like?) Maya smiles. She wants to write back in Spanish. She will need soy, eres, es, somos and son. They are all forms of one verb, ser (to be).
story.think: Lucía used soy, es and somos. What do you think each one means, and how could you tell from the letter?

lessons.title: Soy: Saying Who I Am
lessons.mainIdea: Soy means I am, and you use it to say your name and who you are.
reading: Picture your first day with a new classmate. You point to yourself and say Soy Maya (I am Maya). That one word, *soy*, means I am. It comes from the verb *ser* (to be). A verb is an action or being word.

Look at more examples. Soy Carlos. (I am Carlos.) Soy estudiante. (I am a student.) Soy de Chicago. (I am from Chicago.) Each time, soy tells who you are. You do not need the word yo (I). The ending -oy already says I.
English speakers sometimes say Yo es. That is a mistake. Es goes with he or she. With I, always use soy. Say it aloud: soy, soy, soy. Now say your name after it.

words.d: to be — the verb for who you are, where you are from and what you are like
I am — the yo form of ser: Soy Maya.
the student — Soy estudiante. (I am a student.)

look.title: Two New Friends
look.text:
Ana: ¡Hola! Soy Ana. (Hi! I am Ana.)
Beto: ¡Hola! Soy Beto. Soy estudiante. (Hi! I am Beto. I am a student.)
Ana: Yo también soy estudiante. (I am a student too.)
look.prompt: Say two sentences about yourself with soy: your name and one more thing.

check.q: How do you say I am Sofía in Spanish?
check.why: Soy is the I form of ser. Es means he or she is.

check.q: What does Soy estudiante mean?
check.why: Soy means I am, so Soy estudiante means I am a student.

check.q: Why can you say Soy Carlos without the word yo?
choices: Because yo is a rude word.
Because Carlos is a boy's name.
Because the ending of soy already means I.
Because Spanish has no word for I.
check.why: The verb ending tells who. Soy can only mean I am, so yo is extra.

lessons.title: Eres and Es: You, He, She
lessons.mainIdea: Use eres for you (a friend) and es for he, she or it.
reading: Now you meet a classmate. You ask ¿Eres de Chicago? (Are you from Chicago?) The word *eres* means you are. Use it with tú, the word for you when you talk to a friend or a kid your age.

When you talk about someone else, use *es*. Él es Marco. (He is Marco.) Ella es mi amiga. (She is my friend.) Es also works for things. Es un libro. (It is a book.) One form, es, covers he, she and it.
Watch the endings: soy, eres, es. A common mistake is to say Tú es. Es never goes with tú. Another mistake is to use soy for everyone. Stop and ask: who am I talking about? Then pick the ending.

words.d: you are — the tú form of ser: Eres simpático. (You are nice.)
he is, she is, it is — the él and ella form of ser: Ella es Ana.
you — to a friend, a family member or a kid (with an accent mark)

look.title: Pointing Around the Room
look.text:
Point to yourself: Soy Luis. (I am Luis.)
Point to a friend: Tú eres Ana. (You are Ana.)
Point to a boy: Él es Marco. (He is Marco.)
Point to a girl: Ella es Rosa. (She is Rosa.)
look.prompt: Point to three people in your room and say a sentence about each with soy, eres or es.

check.q: Choose the right word: Tú ___ mi amigo.
check.why: Tú goes with eres. Tú eres mi amigo means You are my friend.

check.q: Choose the right word: Ella ___ de Puerto Rico.
check.why: Ella (she) goes with es. Ella es de Puerto Rico means She is from Puerto Rico.

check.q: What does Él es Marco mean?
check.why: Él means he, and es means is. So Él es Marco means He is Marco.

lessons.title: Somos and Son: Groups
lessons.mainIdea: Use somos for we are and son for they are or you all are.
reading: Picture your soccer team in a photo. You say Somos amigos (We are friends). *Somos* means we are. It goes with nosotros (we). Girls only can say nosotras. Both use somos.
Now point to two other kids. Ellos son hermanos. (They are brothers.) *Son* means they are. It goes with ellos, ellas and ustedes (you all). Ustedes son de Chicago. (You all are from Chicago.)
Now you have all five forms: soy, eres, es, somos, son. Some learners say Nosotros son. That mixes up we and they. Remember: we ends in -mos, like nosotros. Somos and nosotros both end in -mos.

words.d: we are — the nosotros form of ser: Somos amigos.
they are, you all are — the ellos, ellas and ustedes form of ser
we — for a group with at least one boy; nosotras for a group of only girls

look.title: Five Forms of Ser
look.text:
yo soy (I am)
tú eres (you are)
él, ella es (he, she is)
nosotros somos (we are)
ellos, ellas, ustedes son (they are, you all are)
Trick: somos and nosotros both end in -mos.
look.prompt: Cover the list. Can you say all five forms from memory, starting with yo soy?

check.q: Choose the right word: Nosotros ___ de Illinois.
check.why: Nosotros (we) goes with somos. Both end in -mos.

check.q: What does Ellas son hermanas mean?
check.why: Ellas means they (girls), and son means are. So it means They are sisters.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Ustedes (you all) takes son, the same form as ellos.

lessons.title: Soy de Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Ser plus de tells where someone is from: Soy de Chicago.
reading: Lucía wrote Soy de Monterrey. The little word *de* means from. So ser + de + a place tells where a person is from. Soy de Chicago. (I am from Chicago.) Mi abuela es de Guatemala. (My grandma is from Guatemala.)

Use the right form of ser for the person. Tú eres de Texas. (You are from Texas.) Nosotros somos de Illinois. (We are from Illinois.) Ellos son de Colombia. (They are from Colombia.) The place stays the same. Only the verb changes.
English speakers sometimes forget de. They say Soy Chicago. That sounds like I am Chicago! Always put de before the place. Where you are from does not change, so Spanish uses ser for it.

words.d: from, of — Soy de Chicago. (I am from Chicago.)
the city — Monterrey es una ciudad grande. (Monterrey is a big city.)
the country — México es un país. (Mexico is a country.)

look.title: Where Is Our Class From? (example)
look.cite: Example class survey made up for practice, 24 students
look.prompt: How many students in this example class are from somewhere other than Chicago? Say one sentence with son de.

check.q: How do you say I am from Chicago?
check.why: You need ser plus de plus the place: Soy de Chicago.

check.q: Choose the right word: Mis primos ___ de Colombia.
check.why: Mis primos means my cousins, which is they. They takes son.

check.q: Why does Spanish use ser to say where you are from?
choices: Because it is about how you feel.
Because it is about where you are right now.
Because it only works for cities.
Because where you come from does not change.
check.why: Ser is for who you are and things that do not change, like where you are from.

lessons.title: Nationality Words
lessons.mainIdea: Nationality words are lowercase in Spanish and change -o to -a for a girl.
reading: Lucía wrote Somos mexicanos (We are Mexican). A *nacionalidad* (nationality) is a word for what country someone is from. In English we write Mexican with a capital M. In Spanish, mexicano starts with a small m.
Many nationality words end in -o for a boy and -a for a girl. Pedro es mexicano. Rosa es mexicana. Juan es colombiano. Ana es colombiana. For a group, add -s: Ellos son cubanos.

Some words do not change. Estadounidense means from the United States. Él es estadounidense. Ella es estadounidense. It is the same for both. Watch out: do not use a capital letter, and match -o or -a to the person.

words.d: nationality — what country a person is from
Mexican — for a boy or man / for a girl or woman
from the United States — the same word for a boy or a girl

look.title: Match the Ending
look.text:
Pedro es mexicano. Rosa es mexicana.
Luis es puertorriqueño. Ana es puertorriqueña.
Tom es estadounidense. Kim es estadounidense.
Los dos son colombianos. (The two are Colombian.)
look.prompt: Say where you or someone in your family is from with a nationality word. Is it -o, -a or neither?

check.q: Choose the right word: Rosa es ___.
check.why: Rosa is a girl, so the word ends in -a. Nationality words are lowercase.

check.q: Which is spelled the Spanish way?
check.why: In Spanish, nationality words start with a small letter, and a boy takes -o: cubano.

check.q: Kim is a girl from the United States. Which is right?
check.why: Estadounidense is the same for boys and girls, lowercase, and Kim takes es.

lessons.title: Asking ¿De dónde eres?
lessons.mainIdea: Ask ¿De dónde eres? and answer with Soy de and a place.
reading: At a new school you want to know where a friend is from. Ask ¿De dónde eres? (Where are you from?) It starts with the upside-down ¿ and ends with ?. *Dónde* means where. It has an accent mark on the o.
Answer with soy de. ¿De dónde eres? Soy de Chicago. To ask about someone else, change eres to es. ¿De dónde es tu mamá? (Where is your mom from?) Mi mamá es de Honduras. (My mom is from Honduras.)
In English, from goes at the end: Where are you from? Spanish puts de first: ¿De dónde eres? A common mistake is ¿Dónde eres de? Keep de and dónde together at the start.

words.d: from where? — ¿De dónde eres? (Where are you from?)
where — a question word with an accent on the o

look.title: A Quick Interview
look.text:
Nico: ¿De dónde eres? (Where are you from?)
Isa: Soy de Puerto Rico. ¿Y tú? (I am from Puerto Rico. And you?)
Nico: Soy de Chicago. Mi papá es de México. (I am from Chicago. My dad is from Mexico.)
look.prompt: Ask a partner ¿De dónde eres? and answer in a full sentence.

check.q: Which question asks Where are you from?
check.why: Spanish puts de first: ¿De dónde eres? Eres matches tú.

check.q: Someone asks ¿De dónde es tu abuelo? What is a good answer?
check.why: The question is about your grandpa, so answer with es: Mi abuelo es de Cuba.

check.q: What does ¿De dónde es Ana? mean?
check.why: De dónde means from where, so the question asks where Ana is from.

lessons.title: Describing with Ser
lessons.mainIdea: Ser plus a describing word tells what someone is like: Soy alto.
reading: Lucía asked ¿Cómo eres? (What are you like?) To answer, use ser plus a describing word. Soy *alto* (I am tall). Soy cómico (I am funny). A describing word, or adjective, tells about a person or thing.
Describing words match the person. A boy is alto. A girl is alta. Mi hermano es alto. Mi hermana es alta. Some words end in -e and do not change: Él es inteligente. Ella es inteligente.
These words tell what a person is like most of the time. That is why they use ser. A common mistake is to say Soy alta if you are a boy. Check: does the ending match you?

words.d: tall — for a boy / for a girl: Soy alto. Soy alta.
nice, friendly — Mi amiga es simpática.
smart — the same for boys and girls

look.title: ¿Cómo eres?
look.text:
Lucía: ¿Cómo eres? (What are you like?)
Maya: Soy baja y soy cómica. (I am short and I am funny.)
Lucía: ¿Y tu hermano? (And your brother?)
Maya: Mi hermano es alto y simpático. (My brother is tall and nice.)
look.prompt: Answer ¿Cómo eres? with two describing words that match you.

check.q: A boy says: Soy ___ (tall).
check.why: A boy uses the -o ending: Soy alto.

check.q: Choose the right sentence about a girl named Eva.
check.why: Eva takes es, and a girl takes the -a ending: simpática.

check.q: What does ¿Cómo eres? ask?
check.why: With ser, ¿Cómo eres? asks what a person is like.

lessons.title: Jobs with Ser
lessons.mainIdea: Use ser to say someone's job, and leave out un or una: Es maestra.
reading: Lucía wrote Mi papá es maestro (My dad is a teacher). A job is part of who a person is. So jobs use ser. Mi mamá es doctora. (My mom is a doctor.) Yo soy estudiante. (I am a student.)
Notice something new. English says a teacher. Spanish just says maestro, with no un. Él es maestro. Ella es bombera. (She is a firefighter.) Leaving out un or una is normal with a job after ser.
Many jobs change -o to -a. El maestro, la maestra. El doctor, la doctora. Some stay the same, like estudiante. A common mistake is Mi mamá es maestro. Match the ending to the person.

words.d: the teacher — Mi papá es maestro.
the doctor — Mi tía es doctora.
the firefighter — Él es bombero.

look.title: Family Jobs
look.text:
Mi mamá es doctora. (My mom is a doctor.)
Mi papá es cocinero. (My dad is a cook.)
Mi tío es bombero. (My uncle is a firefighter.)
Yo soy estudiante. (I am a student.)
look.prompt: Say the job of two people you know with es and the right -o or -a ending.

check.q: How do you say My mom is a teacher?
check.why: Jobs use ser, and a woman teacher is maestra: Mi mamá es maestra.

check.q: Why do jobs use ser?
choices: Because a job is how you feel today.
Because a job is a place.
Because a job is part of who a person is.
check.why: Ser tells who a person is, and a job is part of that.

check.q: My uncle is a firefighter. Which is right?
check.why: Mi tío is he, so use es, and a man is bombero.

lessons.title: Describing a Friend
lessons.mainIdea: Put ser, where someone is from and what they are like together to describe a friend.
reading: Now Maya writes back to Lucía about her best friend. Mi *amiga* se llama Rosa. (My friend's name is Rosa.) Rosa es de Chicago. Es alta y muy simpática. Each sentence uses a form of ser.

Build a description in three steps. First, say who: Él es mi amigo Leo. Next, say where he is from: Es de Humboldt Park, en Chicago. Last, say what he is like: Es cómico e inteligente. Use y (and) to join words. Before a word starting with i, y becomes e.
Check your work. Is the verb es for one friend? Does each describing word match? Amigo for a boy, amiga for a girl. Read it aloud. If it sounds like a picture of your friend, you did it!

words.d: the friend — a boy friend / a girl friend: Mi amiga es Rosa.
very — Es muy simpática. (She is very nice.)
funny — Mi amigo es cómico.

look.title: Maya Writes Back
look.text:
Querida Lucía (Dear Lucía):
Soy Maya. Soy de Chicago. Soy baja y cómica.
Mi amiga Rosa es alta y muy simpática.
Nosotras somos estudiantes.
¿Cómo es tu hermano? (What is your brother like?)
look.prompt: Write three sentences about a friend: who, where from, and what they are like.

check.q: Maya's friend Rosa is funny. Which sentence is right?
check.why: Rosa takes es, and a girl takes -a: cómica.

check.q: What does Mi amigo es de Humboldt Park mean?
choices: My friend is in Humboldt Park now.
My friend is from Humboldt Park.
My friends are from Humboldt Park.
check.why: Es de plus a place tells where someone is from.

check.q: Leo and Sam are both smart. Which is right?
check.why: Two people are they, so use son, and the describing word adds -s: inteligentes.

review.q: Choose the right word: Yo ___ de Chicago.
review.why: Yo takes soy, the I form of ser.

review.q: Choose the right word: Tú ___ muy simpático.

review.why: Somos means we are, and mexicanos means Mexican.
Nationality words are lowercase, and Ana, a girl, takes -a with es.

review.q: How do you ask a friend Where are you from?
review.why: ¿De dónde eres? asks where you are from. De goes first.

review.q: My dad is a doctor. Which is right?
review.why: Jobs use ser, with no un, and a man is doctor.

review.q: In Lucía's letter, what did Soy de Monterrey tell Maya?
review.why: Ser plus de plus a place tells where a person is from.

choices: Who are you and what are you like?
review.why: Ser answers who someone is and what they are like.

chapters.title: Estar: How and Where I Am
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you tell someone how you feel and where you are, and how do you choose between ser and estar?

story.title: A Day at the County Fair
story.kicker: One long day at the fair, told with a verb for feelings and places.
paragraphs: It is Saturday. Diego and his cousin Sara go to the county fair with Diego's grandma. In the car Sara says ¡Estoy contenta! (I am happy!) Diego says Yo también. Estoy contento. (Me too. I am happy.)

At the fair they ride the Ferris wheel. Sara looks down. ¡Qué alto! (How high!) Diego holds on tight. Estoy nervioso. (I am nervous.) Grandma waves from the ground. Ella está abajo. (She is down below.)

Later they eat corn and look at the pigs and goats. Then Sara cannot find Grandma. ¿Dónde está la abuela? (Where is Grandma?) Diego points. Está en el puesto de limonada. (She is at the lemonade stand.)
At sunset the kids sit on a bench. Grandma asks ¿Cómo están? (How are you?) Sara yawns. Estoy cansada, pero estoy feliz. (I am tired, but I am happy.) Diego is tired too. He says Estoy cansado.
Every feeling and every place today used forms of one verb: estoy, está, estamos, están. That verb is estar (to be). It tells how you are right now and where you are.
story.think: Diego felt happy, then nervous, then tired. Why might Spanish use a special verb for feelings that change during a day?

lessons.title: Estoy: How I Am Right Now
lessons.mainIdea: Estoy means I am, and you use it for how you feel right now.
reading: Picture waking up on a school day. You feel sleepy. You say Estoy cansado (I am tired). *Estoy* means I am. It comes from the verb *estar* (to be). Spanish has two verbs for to be: ser and estar.
Estar tells how you are right now. Estoy bien. (I am fine.) Estoy contenta. (I am happy.) Estoy enfermo. (I am sick.) These feelings can change. By lunch you may not be tired anymore.
Watch the accent. Estoy has none. Say it aloud slowly: es-TOY. A common mistake is Soy cansado for I am tired. Tired is a feeling right now, so use estoy.

words.d: to be — the verb for how you feel and where you are
I am — the yo form of estar: Estoy bien.
fine, well — Estoy bien. (I am fine.)

look.title: A Morning at Home
look.text:
Mamá: ¡Buenos días! (Good morning!)
Diego: Estoy cansado. (I am tired.)
Mamá: ¿Y ahora? (And now?) She hands him pancakes.
Diego: ¡Ahora estoy contento! (Now I am happy!)
look.prompt: How do you feel right now? Say one sentence that starts with Estoy.

check.q: How do you say I am fine?
check.why: Feelings right now use estar, and the I form is estoy.

check.q: What does Estoy enfermo mean?
check.why: Estoy means I am, and enfermo means sick.

check.q: Why do you say Estoy cansado and not Soy cansado?
choices: Because tired is how you feel right now.
Because soy only works for girls.
check.why: Estar is for feelings that can change, like being tired.

lessons.title: The Five Forms of Estar
lessons.mainIdea: Estar has five forms here: estoy, estás, está, estamos, están.
reading: At the fair, Sara asks Diego ¿*Estás* bien? (Are you OK?) Estás goes with tú. Then she talks about Grandma: Ella *está* cansada. (She is tired.) Está goes with él, ella and usted.

For groups, use two more forms. Nosotros estamos en la feria. (We are at the fair.) Ellos están contentos. (They are happy.) Estamos ends in -mos, just like somos and nosotros. Están goes with ellos, ellas and ustedes.
Look at the accent marks: estás, está, están. They put the stress on the last part: es-TÁ. Without the mark, esta means this. So write the accent every time.

words.d: you are — the tú form of estar: ¿Estás bien?
he, she or it is — the él and ella form of estar: Ella está feliz.
we are / they or you all are — Estamos bien. Están cansados.

look.title: Five Forms of Estar
look.text:
yo estoy (I am)
tú estás (you are)
él, ella está (he, she is)
nosotros estamos (we are)
ellos, ellas, ustedes están (they are, you all are)
Three of them carry an accent: estás, está, están.
look.prompt: Say all five forms aloud. Which three have an accent mark?

check.q: Choose the right word: Nosotros ___ contentos.
check.why: Nosotros takes estamos. Both end in -mos.

check.q: Choose the right word: Tú ___ nervioso.
check.why: Tú takes estás, with an accent on the a.

check.q: Which is spelled correctly for She is happy?
check.why: Ella takes está, and it needs the accent mark.

lessons.title: ¿Cómo estás?
lessons.mainIdea: ¿Cómo estás? asks how someone feels, and you answer with estoy.
reading: When you meet a friend in the hall, you ask ¿*Cómo* estás? (How are you?) Cómo means how. Your friend answers with estoy. Estoy bien, gracias. (I am fine, thanks.) Estoy muy bien. (I am very well.) Estoy mal. (I am not well.)
To ask about someone else, change the verb. ¿Cómo está tu hermana? (How is your sister?) Está enferma. (She is sick.) To ask a group, say ¿Cómo están? (How are you all?)
Do not mix this up with ¿Cómo eres? That uses ser and asks what you are like. ¿Cómo estás? asks how you feel today. One small change in the verb makes a different question.

words.d: how? — ¿Cómo estás? (How are you?)
bad, not well — Estoy mal. (I am not well.)

look.title: In the Hallway
look.text:
Ana: ¡Hola, Beto! ¿Cómo estás? (Hi, Beto! How are you?)
Beto: Estoy bien, gracias. ¿Y tú? (I am fine, thanks. And you?)
Ana: Estoy un poco cansada. (I am a little tired.)
Beto: ¿Y cómo está tu hermano? (And how is your brother?)
Ana: Está enfermo. (He is sick.)
look.prompt: Act out this talk with a partner. Change the feelings to match how you really are.

check.q: What does ¿Cómo estás? mean?
check.why: Cómo with estar asks how someone feels.

check.q: A friend asks ¿Cómo estás? Which answer fits?
check.why: Answer about yourself with estoy: Estoy bien, gracias.

check.q: How do you ask How is your mom?
check.why: Your mom is she, so use está. ¿Cómo es? would ask what she is like.

lessons.title: Words for Feelings
lessons.mainIdea: Feeling words like contento, triste, cansado and nervioso go with estar.
reading: Think about the fair. Diego feels many things in one day. Estoy *contento* (I am happy) in the car. Estoy nervioso (I am nervous) on the Ferris wheel. Estoy *cansado* (I am tired) at sunset. Each one is how he is right then.
Here are more feelings. Estoy triste. (I am sad.) Estoy enojado. (I am angry.) Estoy enfermo. (I am sick.) Estoy tranquilo. (I am calm.) All of them use estar because they can change.
Use muy (very) or un poco (a little) to say how much. Estoy muy cansado. Estoy un poco triste. Put muy or un poco right before the feeling word, never after it.

words.d: happy, glad — Estoy contenta. (I am happy.)
tired — Estoy cansado. (I am tired.)
sad — the same for boys and girls: Estoy triste.
nervous — Estoy nervioso antes del examen.

look.title: How Is Our Class Today? (example)
look.cite: Example feelings check-in made up for practice, 24 students
look.prompt: Which feeling has the most students in this example? Say it with Diez estudiantes están…

check.q: Diego is on a tall ride and feels scared. What does he say?
check.why: A feeling right now uses estar, and a boy takes -o: Estoy nervioso.

check.q: What does Estoy un poco triste mean?
check.why: Un poco means a little, and triste means sad.

check.q: Where does muy go in a sentence?
choices: At the end: Estoy cansado muy.
It is never used with feelings.
Right before the feeling word: Estoy muy cansado.
check.why: Muy goes right before the word it changes: muy cansado.

lessons.title: Matching -o and -a
lessons.mainIdea: Feeling words end in -o for a boy, -a for a girl, and add -s for a group.
reading: At sunset Sara says Estoy cansada. Diego says Estoy cansado. They feel the same thing, but the endings differ. Sara is a girl, so she uses -a. Diego is a boy, so he uses -o.
For more than one person, add -s. Ellos están cansados. (They are tired.) Ellas están contentas. (They are happy, all girls.) A mixed group of boys and girls uses -os: Diego y Sara están cansados.

Words ending in -e, like triste, do not change for boy or girl. Él está triste. Ella está triste. For a group they add -s: Están tristes. English speakers often forget the ending because English adjectives never change.

words.d: angry, mad — Mi hermana está enojada.
sick — Los niños están enfermos.

look.title: Same Feeling, Different Endings
look.text:
Diego: Estoy cansado.
Sara: Estoy cansada.
Diego y Sara: Estamos cansados.
Sara y su amiga: Estamos cansadas.
La abuela: Estoy triste. El abuelo: Estoy triste.
look.prompt: Why does Diego y Sara take -os even though Sara is a girl?

check.q: Sara is sick. Which sentence is right?
check.why: Sara takes está, and a girl takes -a: enferma.

check.q: Diego and Sara are angry. Which is right?
check.why: Two people take están, and a mixed group of a boy and a girl uses -os.

check.q: Why does triste not change in Él está triste and Ella está triste?
choices: Because only girls can be triste.
Because words ending in -e stay the same for boys and girls.
check.why: Describing words that end in -e do not change for boy or girl.

lessons.title: Estoy en la escuela
lessons.mainIdea: Estar plus en tells where someone or something is right now.
reading: Where are you right now? Probably in class. You say Estoy en la escuela (I am at school). *En* means in or at. Estar plus en plus a place tells where someone is.
Use the right form for each person. Mi mamá está en el trabajo. (My mom is at work.) Nosotros estamos en la *casa*. (We are at home.) Los perros están en el parque. (The dogs are in the park.)
Here is a surprise. Even places that never move use estar. Chicago está en Illinois. (Chicago is in Illinois.) A common mistake is Chicago es en Illinois. For where a place or person is, use estar.

words.d: in, at, on — Estoy en la escuela.
the school — Estamos en la escuela.
the house, home — Estoy en la casa. (I am at home.)

look.title: Where Is Everyone at 10 a.m.? (example)
look.cite: Example attendance check made up for practice, 24 students
look.prompt: How many students in this example are not at school? Say one sentence with están en.

check.q: How do you say We are at the park?
check.why: Where you are uses estar, and we takes estamos.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: The location of a place uses estar plus en: Chicago está en Illinois.

check.q: What does Mi papá está en la casa mean?
choices: My dad is happy at home.
check.why: Está en la casa tells where he is: at home.

lessons.title: ¿Dónde está?
lessons.mainIdea: Ask ¿Dónde está? to find where someone or something is.
reading: At the fair Sara asked ¿Dónde está la abuela? (Where is Grandma?) Dónde means where. With está it asks where someone is right now. For more than one, use están. ¿Dónde están los niños? (Where are the kids?)

Answer with estar and a place. Está en el puesto. (She is at the stand.) Están en el carro. (They are in the car.) You can also use aquí (here) and allí (there). El libro está aquí. (The book is here.)
Compare two questions. ¿De dónde es? asks where someone is from. It uses ser. ¿Dónde está? asks where someone is now. It uses estar. A trip to the fair changes where you are, not where you are from.

words.d: here — Estoy aquí. (I am here.)
there — La abuela está allí. (Grandma is there.)

look.title: Lost at the Fair
look.text:
Sara: ¿Dónde está la abuela? (Where is Grandma?)
Diego: No está aquí. (She is not here.)
Sara: ¿Está en el puesto? (Is she at the stand?)
Diego: ¡Sí! Está allí, con limonada. (Yes! She is there, with lemonade.)
look.prompt: Pick an object in your room. Ask a partner ¿Dónde está…? and have them answer with aquí, allí or en.

check.q: What does ¿Dónde están los niños? ask?
check.why: Dónde with están asks where people are right now.

check.q: Someone asks ¿Dónde está el libro? Which answer fits?
check.why: Where something is uses estar: Está aquí means It is here.

check.q: Which question asks where Ana is from?
check.why: Where someone is from uses ser and de: ¿De dónde es Ana?

lessons.title: The Rule of Thumb
lessons.mainIdea: How you feel and where you are use estar; who you are and what you are like use ser.
reading: Now you know two verbs for to be. How do you choose? Here is a rule of thumb. How you feel and where you are use estar. Think: estar sounds like state and location. Estoy cansado. Estoy en casa.
Who you are, where you are from and what you are like use ser. Soy Diego. Soy de Chicago. Soy alto. Soy estudiante. These do not change from minute to minute.
Look at one person with both verbs. Sara es alta. (Sara is tall.) Sara está cansada. (Sara is tired.) Tall is what she is like, so use ser. Tired is how she feels today, so use estar.

words.d: to be — who you are, where you are from, what you are like, your job
to be — how you feel and where you are right now

look.title: One Girl, Two Verbs
look.text:
Sara es de Chicago. (where she is from: ser)
Sara es simpática. (what she is like: ser)
Sara está en la feria. (where she is now: estar)
Sara está contenta. (how she feels now: estar)
look.prompt: Write two sentences about yourself: one with soy and one with estoy. Explain why each one fits.

check.q: Which sentence needs estar?
check.why: Tired today is a feeling right now, so it uses estar.

check.q: Choose the right word: Mi hermano ___ alto.
check.why: Tall is what he is like, so use ser: es alto.

check.q: Choose the right word: Mi hermano ___ en la escuela.
check.why: Where someone is uses estar: está en la escuela.

lessons.title: Choosing Ser or Estar
lessons.mainIdea: Ask who or what like for ser, and how or where for estar.
reading: When you are stuck, ask a question about the sentence. Does it answer who? or what is it like? Use ser. Does it answer how do you feel? or where? Use estar.
Try it. Maya ___ de Chicago. Where is she from? That is ser: Maya es de Chicago. Maya ___ en la feria. Where is she now? That is estar: Maya está en la feria. Just one word changes the meaning.
Some learners use es for everything because English uses is for everything. Slow down and check. Is it a feeling or a place? Pick estar. Is it a name, a home country, a trait or a job? Pick ser.

words.d: who? — ser answers it: ¿Quién es? Es mi amiga.
where? — estar answers it: ¿Dónde está? Está aquí.

look.title: Sort the Sentences
look.text:
1. Rosa ___ mi amiga. (who? → es)
2. Rosa ___ contenta hoy. (how does she feel? → está)
3. Rosa ___ de Cuba. (from where? → es)
4. Rosa ___ en la biblioteca. (where now? → está)
5. Rosa ___ inteligente. (what is she like? → es)
look.prompt: Make up one more sentence about Rosa and ask a partner to choose es or está.

check.q: Choose the right word: Hoy yo ___ muy contento.
check.why: How you feel today uses estar, and yo takes estoy.

check.q: Choose the right word: Mis abuelos ___ de Guatemala.
check.why: Where people are from uses ser, and they takes son.

check.q: Why do English speakers often use es where estar is needed?
choices: Because es is shorter to write.
Because English uses one verb, is, for everything.
Because estar is only for girls.
check.why: English has only one verb to be, so learners forget Spanish splits it into ser and estar.

review.q: Choose the right word: Yo ___ cansada.
review.why: Tired is a feeling right now, and yo takes estoy.

review.q: Choose the right word: Ellos ___ en el parque.
review.why: Where people are uses estar, and ellos takes están.
Cómo with estar asks how someone feels.
Where someone is from uses ser, and one friend takes es.

review.q: Which form of estar needs an accent mark?
review.why: Estás, está and están carry an accent. Estoy, estamos and estar do not.

review.q: At the fair, Sara said ¿Dónde está la abuela? What did she want to know?
review.why: Dónde with estar asks where someone is right now.

review.q: Diego and Sara are happy. Which is right?
review.why: Feelings use estar, two people take están, and a mixed group takes -os.
Being a student is who you are, so it uses ser. The others are places or feelings.
